Start Here · Your first 30 days

Learn the business, then work the phones.

Six short sections, in order. Everything else in this portal goes deeper; this track is all you need to make your first good call.
Why we exist · read this first Aging in Georgia is fragmented: the doctor doesn't talk to the caregiver, the caregiver doesn't talk to the family, and the family finds out in the ER. And beneath the fragmentation is a scarcity: there are simply not enough quality, committed home care teams, and the people who need them most — the homebound, the behavioral-health population, small care homes — are often the most neglected communities in medicine, and outside it. Godwins Family Care was founded by a physician and a nurse practitioner — Dr. Bianca Ume and Bethel Godwins, FNP — on one conviction: families deserve a trusted partner who notices subtle changes, coordinates care proactively, and treats every client like our own loved one. Every call you make carries that. You are not selling hours of labor; you are selling the end of "nobody's watching." Our three values — compassion, clinical excellence, integrity — are also your sales rules: never overpromise, never trash a competitor, always follow through on exactly what you said.
Section 1
Words you’ll hear in the first five minutes
NP / FNP — a nurse practitioner, a clinician who can examine, diagnose and manage prescriptions. PCH — personal care home, a small licensed house, usually 3 to 6 residents. ALF — assisted living facility. ILF — independent living, residents live on their own. CCRC — a campus with several levels of care on one site. ADL — activities of daily living: bathing, dressing, eating. LTC — long-term care. LTC insurance is a policy that pays for it. AWV — the annual wellness visit Medicare covers in full.
Full glossary in Section 6.

What GFC sells

Godwins Family Care is two arms of care on one spine, and you sell the whole body on every call.

Arm 1 · Clinical

Medical care that comes to the patient

A nurse practitioner (an "NP", a clinician who can examine, diagnose, and coordinate prescriptions) visits the patient where they live: a facility room, a personal care home, or their own house. Primary care and psychiatric care, including behavioral-health medication management, plus skilled nursing: wound care, injections, catheter and G-tube care, post-surgical observation. Facilities love it because a doctor visit normally costs them half a day: arrange transport, pull a staff member off the floor, exhaust the resident. We erase that trip.

Arm 2 · Home care

Hands-on help at home

Trained caregivers, one on one, for daily living: companionship, bathing, dressing, meals, housekeeping, transportation, up through structured dementia and behavioral support. Families buy this by the hour. The average client uses about 10 to 12 hours a week and stays about a year, which is roughly $16,000 to $18,000 of care over that year. That one number is why your job matters.

The spine: Care Coordination, included with everything.

Whatever a family buys, we talk directly with their physicians, specialists, and therapists, share documentation with the family and the care team, and escalate problems before they become ER visits. This is the sentence that separates us from every agency that just staffs hours: nobody falls through the cracks, because someone is paid to watch the cracks. Facilities hear this as "you make my residents' care legible." Families hear it as "someone is finally driving."

The bench · Psychosocial team

LMSW case management

Licensed master social workers who handle the human side clinical care can't: family conflict, placement decisions, benefits navigation, crisis moments. Two tiers: Standard (monthly advocacy and clinical support) and Intensive (weekly contact, real-time provider coordination, active intervention authority for transitions and crises). Paired with our behavioral-health NP visits, this is a psychosocial capability almost no home care agency in Georgia can match. Lead with it in memory care and any family in chaos.

The bench · Named program

Continuous Care Program

Our monitoring layer: camera-based observation, video check-ins, and a family portal today; Medicare-billed chronic care management and remote patient monitoring phases coming behind it. For a facility, this is "extra eyes between visits." For an adult child two states away, it is the reason they sleep. Sell it as the answer to "what happens when your caregiver isn't there?"

Why it all together wins. Most competitors staff hours or run clinic visits, one or the other, with nobody coordinating. We are physician and FNP owned: the clinical arm, the home care arm, the social workers, and the monitoring program all talk to each other, with care coordination as the connective tissue. When you offer a facility the whole system, you stop sounding like the fifth home care agency to call this month and start sounding like their clinical partner.

One rule covers how we get paid. When the family or their own policy pays us directly, that work is commissioned. When a government or insurance program pays, it is covered by your hourly rate instead. You sell all of it the same way; the difference is bookkeeping, not strategy. The Pay Sheet has the full breakdown when you want it.

One sentence to keep“We bring the doctor's visit, the daily help, and one team coordinating all of it, to the resident.”
Section 2

Who we call, and where

You are selling business to business. The "customer" on the phone is a facility that controls access to many families at once. Sign one facility and you may gain five, ten, forty residents over time. That beats chasing one family at a time, every time.

Your working lane: four counties, worked deep.

Every list you pull and every call you make in your first weeks stays inside these lines. Depth in four counties beats scraps across twenty; these communities talk to each other, and a good visit in Acworth becomes a warm intro in Cartersville. The Targeting Map filters to exactly this footprint. GFC serves all nine counties above and takes referrals beyond them, but the metro Atlanta side comes last. Stay in these four until your calendar earns more.

Your first lanes: six facility types. All are communities where residents live or spend their days, care needs grow on site, and getting people out to appointments is a pain we remove. Learn these six before anything else.

01

Personal Care Homes (PCH)

Our core partner · start here
Small licensed homes, often 6 to 24 beds, usually owner-operated.
Ask for: the owner or administrator; often the same person.
They care about: the cost and chaos of getting residents to outside appointments, and keeping beds filled.
Qualifying question“How do your residents get to their doctor's appointments today?”
Why they're first: one decision-maker, short sales cycle, and our NP visits solve their biggest daily headache.
Full script →📎 Demo deck
02

Adult Day Care Programs

Warm population, easy conversation
Daytime programs seniors attend while family works; participants go home every evening.
Ask for: the program director or owner.
They care about: what happens to participants on evenings, weekends, holidays, and the days they can't come in. We are the other half of their day.
Qualifying question“Do families ever struggle to cover evenings and weekends, or the days their loved one can't make it in?”
Full script →📎 Demo deck
03

Assisted Living Facilities (ALF)

Bigger buildings, real volume
Larger, more structured, sometimes corporate-owned communities.
Ask for: the Executive Director or the Director of Nursing (the "DON").
They care about: resident health events they didn't catch early, family complaints, and staff time.
Qualifying question“Does every resident have a primary care or psychiatric provider actively following them?” If not, that is your opening.
Full script →📎 Demo deck
04

Independent Living (ILF)

Keep the resident in place
Apartments for seniors who mostly manage on their own.
Ask for: the Executive Director or the wellness/activities director.
They care about: residents who start declining. The family's choice becomes "move to assisted living, or get outside help." We are the outside help that lets the resident stay, which keeps the facility's unit occupied.
Qualifying question“Do you have residents starting to need more help than independent living offers?”
Full script →📎 Demo deck
05

CCRCs (Continuing Care Retirement Communities)

Slowest door, biggest prize
One campus holding independent, assisted, and nursing levels together.
Ask for: the Executive Director; expect committees.
They care about: a partner who can serve every level of the campus, from IL wellness to skilled-recovery windows.
Qualifying question“How many levels of care do you have on campus, and who supports residents between levels?”
Pace yourself: one contract can cover the whole campus. Work these steadily; expect months, not weeks.
Full script →📎 Demo deck
06

Memory Care

Our psychiatric arm's natural home
Secured communities, or wings inside ALFs, for residents living with dementia or Alzheimer's.
Ask for: the Executive Director or memory care director.
They care about: psychiatric medication management, behaviors staff can't handle, and families in crisis. Almost nobody else brings psych care into the building.
Talk track in development — check with Bianca before calling these

The easiest yes you can sell: a free seminar. We actively book educational seminars at facilities, because teaching builds the trust that closes sales later. For you this is gold: when a director hesitates on a partnership meeting, a free educational session for their residents and families is a much smaller ask, and it gets us in the building. You book it; Bianca and a partner deliver it.

Visual slot — seminar two-track graphic drops here
Seminar track A · Bianca + Nate

End-of-life planning & final expense

For communities whose residents are working-class or on tighter budgets. Nate is a final expense producer: burial costs, end-of-life policies, protecting family from a bill they can't carry. Practical, dignified, and every family in the room has thought about it.

Offer it when: the home serves mostly Medicaid, waiver, or modest private-pay residents.

Seminar track B · Bianca + Susan

Senior resources & long-term care coverage

For wealthier communities. Susan covers senior resources and long-term care coverage options: what LTC insurance actually pays for, how to activate a policy, what to put in place before a health event.

Offer it when: the community is private-pay, upscale ILF/CCRC, or families ask about "planning ahead."

📎 LTC deck (leave-behind)

How you pitch it“Before we talk about any partnership, we'd love to give your families a free educational session — no selling, just answers. Which lands better with your residents: planning for final expenses, or making long-term care coverage work?” Their answer also tells you the community's economics, which routes everything else you do with them.

What the seminar is, and is not. At its core every session is education about long-term care: what it costs, what coverage really pays for, how to plan before a crisis. Nothing is sold from the stage. The yield is trust with the facility and with families. But good education creates questions, and afterward some families will ask "what would this look like for us?" The three doors below are for those one-on-one follow-ups: the honest places that conversation can land, depending on the family's coverage and readiness. Many attendees land nowhere yet, and that's fine; you now know the building, and they know your name.

Door 1 · The annual wellness visit

Your easiest yes, and the one that fits every room. Medicare covers the annual wellness visit in full, so there is no copay for the resident and nothing billed to the community, and our nurse practitioner comes to them. Each visit covers a medication review, cognitive and depression screening, fall risk, and a written plan that goes to the family and their own doctor. It opens the door to everything else, because once we have seen someone we are already their team.

No cost to anyone · start here

Door 2 · Home care hours

For families with LTC insurance or private funds, the Track B room especially: hands-on daily help, activated through the very coverage the seminar just explained. Care coordination ties it to Door 1 so the caregiver and the NP work as one team.

The family pays us directly

Door 3 · Continuous Care monitoring

For the family that says "we're not ready for care yet." The Continuous Care Program — camera-based observation, video check-ins, the family portal — is the low-cost way to say yes today. Monitoring catches the decline early, and when needs grow, we are already their team.

The "not yet" answer · keeps the door open

Following up with a family one on one? Send the Family deck. Talking to a caseworker or support group? The Social Services deck.

Later lanes, not yet yours: hospital and skilled-nursing discharge desks, LTC insurance brokers, caregiver support groups, and final expense agents. Each has a full script in the library for when your calendar earns them.
Rule 1 · Need first, coverage second

Open on what the family is actually dealing with, never on money. Once you understand the need and have named a fit, ask how care is paid for today. You need the answer before you quote anything, and asking it second rather than first is the difference between a consultation and a sales call.

Rule 2 · A lead isn't real until a meeting is booked

Everything before a booked decision-maker meeting lives in your portal. The meeting is what moves a lead into the CRM. Never enter a lead early.

Section 3

Your week

Your first 30 days live entirely in this portal. The work is one loop, run every working block; master it before you improvise. This is the concept. The operating detail behind it, your systems, hour rules, and the full ninety-day arc, lives in the Liaison Playbook; read it right after this page.

1

Pull your list

Open the Targeting Map, filter to your four counties and your first-lane facility types, and pick 10 to 15 uncontacted facilities. That is today's list. Never dial from memory.
2

Call with the script

Two minutes of prep per facility: name, type, who you're asking for. Then dial, using the flow in Section 4. Video and email touches count, but the phone moves fastest.
3

Log every result, immediately

In the map row: tick Contacted, note the Result, set a Follow-Up date. Ten seconds, every call, no exceptions. If it isn't logged, it didn't happen; your follow-ups, your pay records, and Bianca's view of your work all read from this.
4

Book the meeting, or the seminar

The ask on every call is a decision-maker meeting. If they hesitate, offer the seminar (Section 2). Either one is a win; log which and when.
5

Hand off when it's real

Meeting booked = real lead. Use "→ Notion" on the row; the system creates the CRM records and your follow-up task. From then on your edits sync automatically, and your tasks live in the Tasks panel.
Your scoreboard, weekly.

Week 1: 20 logged conversations. Week 2: your first decision-maker meeting or seminar booked. Month 1: first handoff to the CRM. Month 3: running your own book: prospecting, pipeline, and task board without prompting. These are floors, not ceilings, and they're what we review together each week.

Section 4

The call

One flow for every first call. The full script library has the deep version per vertical; this is the shape you learn first.

1

Open, human and brief

“Hi, this is Jasleen with Godwins Family Care. We're a physician-owned practice that brings primary care, psychiatric care, and home care to communities like yours in the local area. We'd love to connect with you about how we can support your residents' long-term healthcare. Is [the owner / your Executive Director] available?”
Ten seconds. No apology for calling, no "how are you today."
2

Ask the vertical's qualifying question

Each facility card in Section 2 carries one. Ask it, then stop talking. Their answer tells you whether there's a fit and hands you your next sentence.
3

Make the ask, both ways at once

“I'd love to set up a meeting with you and Dr. Ume, or host an in-person lunch and learn or seminar to share long-term care information with your residents. Would next week or the week after suit you better?”
Offer both in one breath. You are not falling back to the seminar when they stall; you are handing them two good doors and letting them pick. Either answer is a win, and you log which one they took.
4

Close the loop

Confirm the next step out loud, thank them by name, and log the call before the next dial.

The four answers you'll hear most, and yours back:

“We already work with an agency.”

“That's great, and keep them. Most of our partners started exactly there; we're usually the clinical layer their agency doesn't have: the NP who comes on site for primary and psych care. Does their team do that?”

“Just send me some information.”

“Happy to. So I send the right thing: is your bigger headache getting residents to appointments, or families needing more support at home? … I'll send that today and call Thursday to see what questions it raised.”

“We're not interested.”

“Understood, and thanks for being straight with me. One thing before I go: we run free educational sessions for residents and families, no selling; would that ever be useful to your community?” If no, log it warmly and move on. No chasing.

The gatekeeper won't put you through.

They're doing their job; make them an ally. “Totally understand. What's the best way to get fifteen minutes on [name]'s calendar, and whom should I address it to?” Get a name, a time, or an email; log which.

Section 5

How you're paid

Four streams. The full Liaison Pay Sheet has every table; this is the plain-words version.

1 · Outreach hours, guaranteed

$18/hour through payroll for scheduled, documented outreach: 6 to 12 hours a week you choose and submit two weeks ahead. This is certain money, and it also covers everything you do in the Program lane (Medicare/Medicaid), where commission is illegal.

2 · Acquisition

A commissioned client's first month: 12% of collected revenue, with a $200 floor so a smaller client still writes a real check.

3 · Retention

Months 2 through 12: 7% monthly ($90 floor) on every client you keep. This is why staying close to families is paid work, not admin.

4 · Ownership

Year 2 onward: 3% monthly. Your book becomes an annuity. Facility partnerships pay their own ladder on top, and concierge (DPC) memberships pay 50% of month 1, 10% in year 1, 5% after.

One client, worked out.

An average client, about 11 hours a week at roughly $1,450 a month, collected: month 1 pays you $200; months 2 to 12 pay $102 each; year 1 totals about $1,320 from that single family, on top of your hours. Close two a month and by month 3 your commissions roughly match your hourly pay; the pay sheet's 90-day table walks it line by line. Everything is paid on collected revenue, never on promises.

Section 6

Glossary

Every term you'll hear in week one. Say them casually and you sound like the industry; stumble and you sound like a cold call.

PCH — Personal Care Home; small licensed residential home, often 6–24 beds.
ALF — Assisted Living Facility; larger licensed community with daily-living support.
ILF — Independent Living; senior apartments, minimal built-in care.
Memory care — secured community or wing for dementia/Alzheimer's residents.
CCRC — Continuing Care Retirement Community; one campus, multiple care levels.
SNF — Skilled Nursing Facility ("sniff"); nursing home for higher medical needs.
ADP — Adult Day Program; daytime care while family works.
ED — Executive Director, the top decision-maker in most communities.
DON — Director of Nursing, the clinical decision-maker.
Discharge planner — hospital/SNF staffer who arranges where a patient goes next.
NP / FNP — Nurse Practitioner / Family NP; examines, diagnoses, coordinates prescriptions.
LMSW — Licensed Master Social Worker; our psychosocial case managers.
ADLs / IADLs — Activities of Daily Living (bathing, dressing, eating) / Instrumental ones (meals, meds, errands).
LTC / LTCi — Long-Term Care / LTC insurance, policies that fund home care.
Medicare — federal health coverage, 65+; pays provider visits, not ongoing home care hours.
Medicaid — state program for limited-income; never commissioned.
Private pay — the family pays directly; commissioned.
DPC / concierge — membership-based enhanced clinical access; commissioned.
Continuous Care Program — our monitoring layer: cameras, video check-ins, family portal.
CCM / RPM — Chronic Care Management / Remote Patient Monitoring; Medicare-billed phases coming to the program above.
Care coordination — our spine: direct provider communication, shared documentation, proactive escalation.
C&P exams — our VA examination division. Not something you sell; route questions to Bianca.
Cold / warm lead — not yet contacted / engaged through calls, meetings, or collateral.
Handoff — the moment a lead with a booked meeting moves from the portal into the CRM (Notion).
CRM — Customer Relationship Management system; ours is Notion.
